– Bussen har sklidd av veien og ut i grøfta med alle fire hjul. I bussen er det 24 barn som fremstår uskadd, skriver operasjonsleder Per Magne Eftang i politiloggen.
Bussjåføren er også uskadd, ifølge politiet.
– Barna er nå på vei ut av bussen og inn et hus for å holde varmen, sier Eftang til NRK.
Han sier alle barna brukte bilbelte.
Operasjonslederen antar at hendelsen kan knyttes til det glatte føret, men politiet har ikke kommet fram til stedet ennå.
Klokka 09.44 opplyser politiet at ingen er skadet. Flere foreldre har hentet barna sine og ny buss er klar til å frakte resten av barna til skolen.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/cnn_-demokratene-vinner-historisk-senatsvalg-i-mississippi-1.18079865</link>
      <description>Demokraten Scott Colom har vunnet senatsvalget i den tradisjonelt republikanske delstaten Mississippi, ifølge CNNs prognose.
Colom slår dermed den sittende republikanske senatoren Cindy Hyde-Smith, melder CNN onsdag kveld.
Han blir den første demokraten som representerer Mississippi i Senatet på over 40 år.
Colom blir også den første svarte politikeren som velges til et politisk verv av velgerne i hele Mississippi siden gjenoppbyggingsperioden etter den amerikanske borgerkrigen på 1800-tallet.
Valget ble holdt 3. november, men opptellingen har trukket ut i over en uke. Onsdag ettermiddag ledet Colom med rundt 3000 stemmer da om lag 98 prosent av stemmene var talt opp.
Resultatet er ennå ikke formelt godkjent. Fylkene i delstaten har frist til fredag med å godkjenne sine valgresultater.
(NTB)</description>

      <description>Klimaminister Sigrun Aasland (Ap) har med en stor sum når hun mandag reiser til åpningen av klimatoppmøtet i Tyrkia.
– Vi har med 600 millioner kroner til Brasil, for de har levert veldig gode resultater på å hindre avskoging i 2025, sier Aasland.

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/kongen-fullforte-maraton-pa-tiden-4.43.01-1.18076803</link>
      <description>Kongen og kronprinsessen er deltakere i French Riviera Marathon, i Nice sør i Frankrike.
Kong Haakon løp i mål på tiden 4.43.01, ifølge sporingstjenesten Trackanza.
Det var TV 2 som meldte saken først.
Et bilde viser kongen og kronprinsessen løpende ved siden av hverandre under maratonet. I maratonet er kronprinsessen registrert som Ingrid Alexandra og kongen som Haakon Magnus.
Startskuddet gikk klokka 09.16, og distansen er helmaraton på 42,125 kilometer. Løypen går langs den franske rivieraen fra Nice til Cannes.
Lørdag formiddag opplyste Slottet på nettsidene sine at «statsrådet forestår bestyrelsen av riket».
Ifølge nettsidene var kongen og kronprinsessen på privat opphold i utlandet. Det betyr at regjeringen har ansvaret for å styre og forvalte landet.
(NTB/NRK)</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/ny-norsk-gulltriumf-i-vm-i-skyting-1.18076796</link>
      <description>Caroline Finnestad Lund, Jeanette Hegg Duestad og Synnøve Berg tok laggullet på 50 meter rifle match i VM i skyting i Doha søndag.
Det var Lunds andre gull i mesterskapet. Lørdag ble 21-åringen verdensmester på 50 meter 60 skudd liggende.
Norge sanket totalt 1764 poeng under lagkonkurransen, og de kom 3,0 poeng foran Sveits på 2.-plass. Tsjekkia stakk av med bronsemedaljen. De var to poeng bak sveitserne igjen.
I eliminasjonen for lag 1 ble Finnestad Lund nummer fire med 588 poeng. Synnøve Berg ble nummer sju med 586 poeng. Duestad ble nummer tre med 590 poeng i lag 2.
Alle de tre norske jentene er videre til kvalifiseringen i den individuelle konkurransen i den samme øvelsen mandag. (NTB)</description>

      <title>Flere skadet etter kraftig jordskjelv sentralt i Japan</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/flere-skadet-etter-kraftig-jordskjelv-sentralt-i-japan-1.18076688</link>
      <description>Minst 22 personer ble skadet da et jordskjelv med styrke 5,5 rammet Shizuoka-prefekturet i det sentrale Japan. Butikkvinduer ble knust, og folk rømte ut av bygninger.
Ifølge kringkasteren NHK er det ikke fare for tsunamier.
Skjelvet inntraff rundt klokka 1 natt til søndag. Det hadde en dybde på 41 kilometer. Den foreløpige målingen fra Japans meteorologiske institutt, som har ansvaret for overvåking og varsling av jordskjelv, var på 5,7.
Det amerikanske jordskjelvsenteret USGS målte det til 5,5.
I naboprefekturet Aichi ble det målt kraftige rystelser på nivå 5+ på den japanske skalaen – det sterkeste som er registrert der siden 1997.
(NTB)</description>
      <category>Japan</category>

      <title>Eisenkot får i oppdrag å danne regjering i Israel</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/eisenkot-far-i-oppdrag-a-danne-regjering-i-israel-1.18076617</link>
      <description>Israels president har gitt opposisjonsleder Gadi Eisenkot i oppdrag å prøve danne regjering.
Hverken partiene som støtter statsminister Benjamin Netanyahu eller partiene som støtter Eisenkot fikk flertall ved valget 27. november.
Netanyahus blokk fikk 53 plasser i Knesset, mens blokken til Eisenkot fikk 48 mandater.
For å få flertall og bli statsminister trenger man 61 plasser i nasjonalforsamlingen. Begge blokkene er avhengig av de 19 mandatene fra de palestinsk-arabiske partiene, mend både Netanyahu og Eisenkot har sagt de ikke vil forhandle med dem.</description>

]]>

An orange-level rainfall warning remains in effect for large swathes of Vancouver Island on Thursday, while some communities face flooding and road closures.

A rainfall warning is in effect for West and Inland Vancouver Island, where 150 to 250 millimetres of rain is forecast to fall Thursday morning, according to Environment Canada.

The rain is expected to ease throughout the day, followed by a “weaker weather system” starting again Thursday night and Friday.

“Localized flooding is likely. Some roads may become impassable,” warned Environment Canada Thursday morning. “Visibility will likely be suddenly reduced at times. Landslides may occur in vulnerable areas such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars.”

Meanwhile, a yellow-level rainfall warning is in effect for East Vancouver Island, from Nanoose Bay to Fanny Bay.

Environment Canada is forecasting 50 to 100 millimetres of rain to fall in this region on Thursday morning, before the weather system weakens later in the day.

The weather office is also warning of water pooling in low-lying areas and potential drops in visibility and landslides for the East Vancouver Island region.

On Wednesday, the Environment Canada weather station at the Port Alberni Airport recorded 123 millimetres of rain.

Last week, Environment Canada meteorologist Steve Boily put the rainfall totals in perspective, saying typically Campbell River gets an average of 220 millimetres during the entire month of November, while Comox receives about 190 for the month.

Nearly one year ago today, Environment Canada introduced a new colour-coded weather alert system, with yellow alerts being the least severe, followed by orange and red alerts.

Yellow alerts are the most common and are issued when weather impacts are “likely moderate, localized, and/or short-term” – while orange alerts are issued when “significant” damage or disruptions are anticipated, with impacts expected to be “major, widespread, and/or may last a few days.”

Active emergency alerts

Evacuation orders and alerts remain in effect for Zeballos after first being issued on Nov. 6 due to flooding and potential landslide risks.

The Strathcona Regional District (SRD) said it expected the emergency measures to remain in place until at least Friday.

Meanwhile, a road closure was issued in the Village of Sayward around the intersection of Sayward Road at Kelsey Way due to flooding on Wednesday. The SRD also issued a water conservation notice for Sayward after the village’s water treatment plant went offline due to sediment in the water coming from high flows in Newcastle Creek.

The Huu-ay-aht First Nation warned of road flooding along Bamfield Main Road on Wednesday, while people in the Port Alberni area were busy preparing sandbags due to flooding.

The Royal Canadian Navy (RCN) is offering free tours of its new vessel, HMCS Robert Hampton Gray, which is now stationed at CFB Esquimalt.

The tours are available on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. at Ogden Point’s Pier B.

While the tours are free, the Greater Victoria Harbour Authority (GVHA) notes that people must register to join one.

HMCS Robert Hampton Gray arrived in Victoria on Nov. 6, after completing an 83-day deployment through the Canadian Arctic.

The ship is an Arctic patrol vessel that departed Halifax and sailed to Greenland and Alaska before arriving at its new home port in Esquimalt, the first time ever an RCN ship relocated from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

RELATED: CFB Esquimalt welcomes new vessel following historic Arctic expedition

“It is only the third time that a Canadian warship has gone through the Northwest Passage,” Cdr Brian Henwood, Commanding Officer of HMCS Robert Hampton Gray, said on Nov. 6.

During its voyage, the vessel participated in training and operations alongside the Canadian Coast Guard, Royal Danish Navy and French Navy.

“The vessel is named after Canadian naval hero Robert Hampton Gray who was awarded the Victoria Cross for leading an airstrike on a Japanese destroyer in World War II,” said the GVHA in a social media post Tuesday. “Gray was the last Canadian killed in action in that conflict.”

As an Arctic patrol vessel, HMCS Robert Hampton Gray is also able to break through ice.

]]> 1360725 His wife died by suicide. He wants the government to reconsider its MAID bill https://cheknews.ca/his-wife-died-by-suicide-he-wants-the-government-to-reconsider-its-maid-bill-1360722/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:24:35 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1360722

If MAID was an option, David Slater said, his wife could have been surrounded by family when she died.

The post His wife died by suicide. He wants the government to reconsider its MAID bill appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

Poring over photographs spilled across his kitchen table, David Slater picks one up that captured his late wife mid-laughter. 

She’s posing at an ancient temple in Greece, holding out a navy skirt in one hand, as if preparing for a curtsy. There are dozens more like it: Diane McDowell draped in a pink pashmina outside the Taj Mahal; sunglasses hanging from her neck as she grins with a family of elephants in Botswana. 

Travel was an escape from the depression she kept at bay for decades with therapy, medication and exploration. “She had kept it in remission,” as Slater put it. “But when the time came, it wasn’t going to go back. She had passed the point of remission.”

Things she once loved — gardening for hours in her Toronto backyard, slipping on a pair of shiny loafers, sailing through the Caribbean — became reminders of her lost joy, out of reach. 

McDowell, 71, wanted a medically assisted death, but was not eligible, Slater said.

She died by suicide on Oct. 25. 

Slater recalls a conversation they had about a month and a half earlier, when his wife of 36 years said, “I don’t want to die, but I don’t want to live like this.” He pauses as a rush of tears spills from his eyes. “And that’s MAID in a nutshell.” 

He believes MAID should be an option for mental illness, and he wants members of Parliament to consider the potential consequences of new legislation introduced by Justice Minister Sean Fraser in late October, which, if passed into law in the coming months, would ban people with mental illness as a sole underlying condition from accessing MAID.

Slater said he knows his wife’s life would have ended either way, but with MAID, “the dignity with which she lived her life would have been maintained.”

The justice minister read McDowell’s obituary and was moved by the tragedy. He recently lost a friend who also struggled with mental illness. However, Fraser said he had to make a decision on MAID in the absence of consensus from the medical community, and erred on the side of caution because of the permanence of the decision to end one’s life.

“And you do your best to, in the presence of a wide range of opinions, take decisions that have the potential to preserve life where possible, without being inconsiderate towards people who don’t see a path for themselves,” Fraser told The Canadian Press in a quiet room on Parliament Hill. 

“People whose experience has been characterized by extraordinary pain and suffering, but who I can’t say with certainty, after having spoken to experts and people with lived experience, that there’s not a possibility for a recovery.” 

Fraser said he was heeding concerns from many psychiatrists who said there was no way to parse out if someone could get better with the right treatment, even if it appeared they had tried everything. He also said he spoke to people who would not be alive today if MAID had been an option, and were happy to still be here.

Some experts in the field, meanwhile, have warned that restricting access to MAID for mental illness would result in people dying by suicide, instead of surrounded by family on their own terms. Obituaries published over the past several years, during which a planned expansion of MAID access was delayed, suggest there have been such cases.

Fraser said this policy decision was not “an accounting exercise,” weighing the fatal stakes of either withholding or granting MAID to people with mental illness. 

“I’m not blind to the struggle that people have when they live with mental illness with deadly consequences,” Fraser said, pausing and becoming visibly emotional as he spoke about his close childhood friend, who he lost just weeks ago after a more than 20-year battle with mental illness. They had grown apart as adults, but remembers him as smart, funny, and talented, on a path to immense success before his life changed. 

“And they tried everything, too,” he said, speaking of his friend and clarifying that MAID was not a part of his story. 

MCDOWELL’S STORY

Depression was a part of McDowell’s life before she met Slater in her early thirties. She managed it with medication and therapy. Slater says she was quieter at low periods, but never cancelled social plans or missed a day at the litigation firm, where she was a founding partner and worked for more than 30 years. At the office, she had a reputation for her grace, empathy and professionalism.

McDowell retired from the law firm in 2012. The couple did not have children — “we have holidays,” Slater said they liked to quip. 

They spent the winters sailing the Caribbean, summers back home in Toronto, and then rented an apartment for about three months in the south of France. 

McDowell’s father was in the Air Force and she lived in Germany, France and across Canada throughout her childhood. She was one of the first in her family to graduate from university and managed the pub at Queen’s University to pay for summer travels, Slater said with pride. 

Several years into retirement, feeling good in her golden years, McDowell asked her family doctor to go off of her medication for depression and began tapering her dose, her husband said.

They were on a boat in Grenada when she woke up one morning and told Slater she had to go home. “Something is not right,” he recalls her saying. That was the beginning of this “more difficult journey.”

She immediately went back on medication. It didn’t help, nor would any of the treatments her doctors tried in the coming years, including transcranial magnetic stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy or ketamine.

“It came on like a ton of bricks. It was shocking,” he said.

Slater recalls waking one night to the sound of their brass headboard banging against the wall. “She was shaking so hard that I thought she was actually having an epileptic fit,” he said. 

He later learned she had had an anxiety attack. It sometimes took eight or nine hours for her surge of panic to subside.

“They say the actual attacks are usually like only four or five minutes, but it’s the getting over them that takes a huge drain,” he said.

Six months after Grenada, McDowell spent a month in the psychiatric ward at Toronto General Hospital. Not long after she was discharged, Slater recalls his wife — someone who would not even answer the door in sweatpants— not getting dressed.

“It took me a long time to understand. Probably. I knew she was ill and, you know, you’ve heard the old, ‘oh, just snap out of it.’ Well, there’s no snapping out of it. And why would a woman who has had the life she had — had the most amazing retirement — why would she choose to lie on the bed and suffer?”

It finally sunk in, he said. His wife had a fatal illness.

She spent another three months back in the psychiatric ward under intense supervision, balancing medications and lots of one-on-one therapy. She also went toHomewood Health Centre, a mental health treatment facilityin an old mansion on a river in Guelph, for about nine weeks. 

“There was no stone left unturned,” Slater said.

“When things really started to look poor, she did talk about MAID. I would have supported her in that. I told her I would,” he added. MAID was not unfamiliar to Slater. His father received the end-of-life procedure at the age of 89 after a stroke.

“My dad’s quality of life, when he was approved, was way better than Diane’s quality of life when she wasn’t even allowed to apply,” he said.

But as a lawyer and a pragmatic person who read the newspaper every day, McDowell knew she was not eligible, and she was not hopeful that would change in the near future.

They looked at going to Switzerland, which has an end-of-life program that receives international applicants. McDowell feared she would be hospitalized again if her doctors found out she wanted MAID.

FUNERAL REMARKS BY MP

McDowell’s funeral took place Nov. 7 and everyone — from her psychiatrist to her hairdresser — showed up, along with Liberal member of Parliament Robert Oliphant, her neighbour for 16 years on their midtown cul-de-sac.

Oliphant co-chaired a parliamentary committee tasked with making recommendations to the government on MAID in 2016. He spoke at McDowell’s funeral, saying he would commit once again to drawing attention to and pushing for fair and rightful access to MAID for people with mental illness.

“Diane’s death is something that I think makes it, again, personal for me,” Oliphant said in an interview from his house, kitty-corner from where she lived.

Soon, he is to vote on the government’s MAID legislation.It won’t be a straightforwarddecision, he said, as a vote in favour would close the door on mental illness but open the door to advance requests for people with dementia and other conditions that take away their capacity to consent. “I will have to decide on where ultimately I come down on it,” he said. 

“Maybe it does take the death of an innocent person to spark us to say, no, we have to help this to not happen to another person.”

‘IT COULD HAVE BEEN DIGNIFIED’

If MAID was an option, Slater said, his wife could have been surrounded by family when she died. They could have talked about the little café they adored on the back side of the Notre-Dame, where they would end up at 2 a.m. for an ice cream and coffee after wandering the streets of Paris. 

“The fact that I couldn’t sit and talk to her about that on her deathbed. You know? That’s wrong,” he said.

He imagines that she would have said, “I do not want to do this, but I have to because I have no choice. She would’ve said, ‘I love you very much.’ I could have held her hand,” he said, breaking into a deep, sorrowful sob.  

“It could have been dignified.”

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.

Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that “all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, said that “while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” he added.

The tomb is considered one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S. and it houses the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II, and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the U.S. Army’s 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as “The Old Guard,” since 1948.

Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that was also attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

The incident comes less than a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress on Tuesday afternoon.

The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth’s critics were not successful in Tuesday’s vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach the defense secretary. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Meanwhile, Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes.

“On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime,” Hegseth said on Tuesday morning.

“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth argued. “This is sabotage.”
